name: Hard-easy effect
statement: Confidence exceeds accuracy on hard sets of questions and falls short of it on easy ones, and little of the pattern is left once two measurement artefacts are removed.
meaning: The paradigm is a two-alternative general knowledge question answered with a confidence report on a scale from .5 to 1.0. Over/underconfidence is defined as mean confidence minus proportion correct. Plot that score against proportion correct across studies and the line slopes down, crossing zero near a proportion correct of .75. Judges look overconfident on hard item sets and underconfident on easy ones. The psychological reading is that confidence tracks difficulty too weakly. The statistical reading is that proportion correct sits on both axes, so the two quantities move against each other whatever the judges are doing.

origin.note: Their paper is titled "Do those who know more also know more about how much they know?". It is closed access, no repository copy was located through Unpaywall or OpenAlex, and this entry did not obtain it. Its finding is reported here from Juslin, Winman and Olsson. They write that Lichtenstein and Fischhoff found overconfidence for item sets with a proportion correct below about .75, and underconfidence above it. The same effect travels as the difficulty effect, after Griffin and Tversky, and as the discriminability effect, after Ferrell and McGoey.

evidence: Juslin, Winman and Olsson assembled the data available to them in June 1998 from studies using two-alternative general knowledge items and the half-range confidence scale. They had 95 independent data points from selected item samples and 35 from representative samples, where items were drawn at random from a defined natural environment. Mean confidence was .73 under both methods, with 95% confidence intervals of plus or minus .01 and .02. Proportion correct was .64 for selected samples and .72 for representative ones. Over/underconfidence was .09 for selected samples and .01 for representative ones, each with a 95% interval of plus or minus .02. Regressing over/underconfidence on proportion correct gave a slope of -.72 for the selected samples, with proportion correct accounting for 70% of the variance, and -.53 for the representative samples, accounting for 58%. That downward slope is the hard-easy effect, and it appears under both methods of choosing items.

replication.headline: The pattern in raw data is not in dispute; the two analyses that removed the statistics producing it found nothing left.
replication.detail: Juslin, Winman and Olsson name three mechanisms that produce the slope without any judge being biased. The confidence scale ends at .5 and 1.0, so response error near the ends can push in only one direction. Proportion correct appears in both the predictor and the outcome, which they call linear dependency and which forces a negative correlation by itself. Confidence and accuracy are only correlated, so each regresses on the other, a line of argument they trace to Erev, Wallsten and Budescu. They corrected the 17 representative samples collected in their own laboratory. Uncorrected, the slope was -.63, 95% CI plus or minus .31, with proportion correct accounting for 51% of the variance. Correcting for scale-end effects alone left -.41 and 31%. Correcting for linear dependency alone left -.42 and 23%, using Klayman, Soll, González-Vallejo and Barlas's method of splitting each sample into a definition set and a measurement set. Correcting for both left a slope of -.20, 95% CI plus or minus .27, with proportion correct accounting for 6% of the variance. The corrected model predicts overconfidence of .03 at a proportion correct of .5 and underconfidence of .06 at a proportion correct of 1.0. Juslin and colleagues report that Klayman and colleagues, applying the same correction across eight topics of general knowledge items, also found no reliable hard-easy effect remaining. Merkle later derived necessary and sufficient conditions for observing the effect. He concluded that judges show it in almost all realistic situations. That includes judges perfectly calibrated at the item level, and judges whose confidence is unrelated to the questions. On his account the pattern is real and tells a researcher nothing about how confidence is produced.

study.cite: Juslin, P., Winman, A., & Olsson, H. (2000). Naive empiricism and dogmatism in confidence research: A critical examination of the hard-easy effect. Psychological Review, 107(2), 384-396.

limits: Everything above concerns two-alternative general knowledge items scored on the half-range scale, which is one paradigm. Juslin, Winman and Olsson argue that scale-end effects, linear dependency and regression apply across judgement research, and their review does not test that. Their corrections were applied to 17 samples from a single laboratory, doubled to 34 points by swapping the roles of the definition and measurement sets. They warn that the corrections are stacked on top of each other and that each carries assumptions. Merkle's derivation rests on a response-error model with a variance of .03 and on true probabilities drawn from a beta distribution, and he states that a beta distribution cannot generally produce multimodal cases. Lichtenstein and Fischhoff's 1977 paper and Klayman and colleagues' 1999 paper were not obtained, so what they found is quoted here from Juslin, Winman and Olsson rather than read. This entry searched Crossref for later work naming the hard-easy effect, and searched the open web for a reanalysis that controls these artefacts and still recovers it. None was located.
misreadings: The effect is not a property of a judge. Merkle shows that both perfectly calibrated judges and judges whose confidence is unrelated to the stimulus produce it, so its presence cannot separate good judges from bad ones. Nor does it show that people cannot tell a hard test from an easy one. Merkle reports that Gigerenzer, Hoffrage and Kleinbölting found judges fairly accurate when asked outright how many questions they had got right. The inaccuracy shows up only when accuracy is inferred from item-by-item confidence. A single pair of tests settles nothing in either direction, and Merkle notes that Gigerenzer and colleagues discussed two studies yielding four apparent reversals of the effect, which the covariance that defines it can absorb. The effect has also been used as an argument rather than a finding. Griffin and Tversky held that the difficulty effect explained away Gigerenzer and colleagues' result that representative item sampling removes overconfidence. Juslin, Winman and Olsson matched hard samples on difficulty, both sets at a proportion correct of .65. Over/underconfidence was .10 for 29 selected samples and .05 for 12 representative ones, so difficulty does not account for the gap.
